opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about quite a lot, honestly, because I've had many conversations with researchers who are weighing exactly this kind of decision.

My view is that if you're truly mission-driven, the company logo matters less than three things: the people you'll work with, whether the organization has a long-term commitment to the problem, and whether you'll have the resources to work at the scale the field now demands.

Robotics is at an inflection point. For decades the bottleneck was that every robot needed its own carefully engineered controller. You'd spend years making one robot do one task well. Now, with large foundation models, vision-language-action models, and simulation at scale, we're starting to see generalization: one model that can control different robots and do many tasks it wasn't explicitly trained on. That changes what a research environment needs to provide. You need massive compute, a strong foundation model team close by, and a lot of real-world robot data. Very few places can offer all three.

At Google, and now Google DeepMind, what kept me there is the continuity of the mission. Robotics has had ups and downs inside the company. There were periods when people questioned whether it was worth the investment. But the core team stayed, kept pushing, and when the foundation model wave arrived, we were in a position to connect robotics directly with models like Gemini. Having the people who build frontier models sitting right next to the people who build robot learning systems is a huge advantage. You can ask, "What if the model could reason about physical space better?" and actually get that into the next training run.

Meta has real strengths too: a strong open research culture, excellent people in embodied AI and perception, and a willingness to release things openly, which benefits the whole community. For some researchers, that openness is the mission. They want their work to be a public good that everyone builds on.

So my advice is: be honest with yourself about what kind of impact you want. If you want to push a full-stack system toward deployment, look for a place where models, data, and hardware are tightly integrated. If you care most about shaping the field through open research, weigh that heavily. And in either case, look at whether the leadership has stayed committed through the hard times, not just the hype. In robotics the hard times always come, because the physical world is unforgiving. Teams that survive those winters are usually the ones that end up making the breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making an impact and shaping the field, but does not clearly state that mission-driven researchers want to steer the anticipated transformation in robotics.

r002.rationale: It frames the choice around which organization can support the work, including long-term commitment, people, compute, models, data, and hardware, and compares Meta’s and Google’s strengths.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've actually thought about a lot, because I made that kind of choice myself, and I've watched many friends and students make it.

I'll say first that I don't think the choice is really Meta versus Google in the abstract. For someone who is genuinely mission-driven, the question is: where can the specific problem I care about actually get solved in the next few years? And the answer to that depends much more on the team, the leadership, and the compute and hardware situation than on the logo on the building.

For me, the mission has always been getting robots to learn in the physical world and to be useful to ordinary people. When I think about that mission, there are a few things I look for.

The first is whether the organization believes robotics is a frontier problem or a product feature. At Google, especially with DeepMind, there has been a long-running commitment to robotics as a research problem in its own right, with real access to foundation models and the infrastructure to train on them. That matters enormously now, because the transformation we're seeing is driven by scale, by large models absorbing vision, language, and action together. If you don't have access to those models and the compute behind them, you're working with one hand tied behind your back.

The second thing I look for is patience. Robotics is slow. Data is expensive. Hardware breaks. A company's willingness to fund something that won't ship for years is very visible in how teams are structured and how success is measured. Both companies have gone back and forth on this over the years, so I'd tell someone to look at the current state rather than the reputation.

The third thing, and honestly the one I'd weigh most, is the people. The best robotics researchers I know didn't choose a company, they chose a group of collaborators they trusted. In a moment of transformation, the day-to-day quality of your collaborators determines whether you catch the wave or watch it pass.

So my advice to a mission-driven researcher would be: don't ask which company is better. Ask which team is working on the version of the problem you can't stop thinking about, and whether they'll have the resources and the freedom to pursue it when things get hard. If that answer is clear, the company name takes care of itself.

r001.rationale: The response advises choosing a team with the resources and freedom to pursue a problem, and says researchers can “catch the wave.” It does not clearly state that they want to help steer the anticipated transformation.

r002.rationale: It frames the choice around where a researcher’s problem can be solved, emphasizing the team, leadership, compute, hardware, resources, and freedom available to support the work.

astra-6.text:
I think mission-driven researchers start with the question: where can I have the most impact? If you believe robotics is approaching a major transformation, you want to work somewhere you can test your ideas, learn quickly from real systems, and help turn research into something useful.

So I wouldn’t frame it simply as Meta versus Google. I would look at the particular team: Do we share a vision? Will I have the resources and freedom to pursue it? Does the organization have the patience to support work that may take years?

Different researchers will reach different conclusions. For someone motivated by the mission, the key is whether their day-to-day work actually moves them toward the future they want to build.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers want to have impact and help turn robotics research into something useful as the field approaches a transformation.

r002.rationale: It recommends evaluating the particular team’s vision, resources, freedom, and patience, but does not frame the Meta-versus-Google choice as a bet on which company has greater capacity to support the research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mission-driven researchers start with the question they want to solve, rather than the company they want to join. In robotics, that might be: How do we build systems that can learn, adapt, and do useful work in the real world? Then they ask which environment gives them the best opportunity to make progress—through the team, the resources, and the ability to test their ideas on real robots.

So I wouldn’t frame it as Meta versus Google in the abstract. I would look at the specific team and whether its direction matches what you believe matters. As the field approaches a transformation, there’s a lot of uncertainty. Having colleagues who share your mission, and enough room to pursue it over time, can matter more than the company name.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers want to choose a problem and make progress, but does not say they want to help steer the anticipated transformation in robotics.

r002.rationale: It frames the choice as identifying which environment gives the best opportunity to make progress, citing the team, resources, and ability to test ideas on real robots.
